content: Acupuncture involves the insertion of very fine needles into specific points on the body, while acupressure uses the application of pressure with the thumbs or fingers to these same points. Both techniques are considered complementary therapies, and their use has been increasing among pregnant women seeking alternatives to conventional medical practices during pregnancy and childbirth. Observational studies to date suggest that acupuncture for labor induction does not appear to have adverse effects on the fetus and may be effective, but the clinical evidence supporting its effectiveness remains limited. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture and acupressure for cervical ripening or labor induction during the third trimester of pregnancy. The review included 22 randomized controlled trials involving 3,456 women. These trials compared acupuncture or acupressure with usual care, sham controls, or other labor induction methods. When comparing acupuncture to sham controls, there was no significant difference in the rate of cesarean sections (average risk ratio [RR] 0.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.56 to 1.15, eight trials, 789 women; high-quality evidence). One trial reported no maternal or perinatal deaths. Acupuncture showed a benefit in improving cervical readiness for labor, as measured by the Bishop's score, within 24 hours (mean difference [MD] 0.40, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.69, one trial, 125 women). However, there was no evidence of differences between groups for outcomes such as oxytocin augmentation, epidural analgesia, instrumental vaginal birth, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, low Apgar scores, neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission, maternal infection, postpartum bleeding, labor duration, or spontaneous vaginal birth. When acupuncture was compared to usual care, there was no clear difference in cesarean section rates (average RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.17, eight trials, 760 women; low-quality evidence). Electro-acupuncture appeared to improve cervical maturation (MD 1.30, 95% CI 0.11 to 2.49, one trial, 67 women) and was associated with a shorter labor duration compared to usual care (MD 124 minutes, 95% CI 37.39 to 210.61, one trial, 67 women). Subgroup analysis suggested that electro-acupuncture may be more effective than manual acupuncture in reducing cesarean section rates (average RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.80, three trials, 327 women) and increasing rates of instrumental vaginal birth (average RR 2.30, 95% CI 1.15 to 4.60, two trials, 271 women) and spontaneous vaginal birth (average RR 2.06, 95% CI 1.20 to 3.56, one trial, 72 women). However, these subgroup findings should be interpreted cautiously due to their observational nature. No significant differences were observed for other outcomes, including oxytocin augmentation, epidural use, low Apgar scores, NICU admission, maternal infection, perineal tears, fetal infection, maternal satisfaction, use of other induction methods, or postpartum bleeding. In a single trial comparing acupuncture to membrane sweeping, there were no significant differences in cesarean section rates (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.22, one trial, 207 women; moderate-quality evidence) or other outcomes such as augmentation, epidural use, instrumental vaginal birth, low Apgar scores, NICU admission, or postpartum bleeding. For acupressure, when compared to sham controls, there was no evidence of benefit in reducing cesarean section rates (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.30, two trials, 239 women; moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, no clear benefits were observed for outcomes such as oxytocin augmentation, instrumental vaginal birth, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, labor duration, or spontaneous vaginal birth. When acupressure was compared to usual care, there was no evidence of benefit in reducing cesarean section rates (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.53, two trials, 151 women; moderate-quality evidence) or other outcomes, including epidural use, low Apgar scores, NICU admission, labor duration, use of other induction methods, or spontaneous vaginal birth. In conclusion, there was no clear evidence that acupuncture or acupressure reduces cesarean section rates. Acupuncture showed some potential benefit in improving cervical maturity, but the quality of evidence varied from low to high across studies. Few trials reported on critical outcomes such as neonatal morbidity or maternal mortality. Further well-designed trials are needed to assess the clinical effectiveness and safety of these techniques, including their impact on relevant maternal and neonatal outcomes.
